title: Medhā devī: the hymn to understanding
theme: Two verses to Medhā, the goddess of understanding and memory: may she come, and by her favour may we speak of the highest; by her favour one becomes a seer, a Brahmā, prosperous.

words.meaning: Medhā, the power to grasp and retain
words.context: The anonymous commentator: «ग्रन्थतदर्थयोर्धारणशक्तिर्मेधा» — the power to retain a text and its meaning
The anonymous commentator: the deity presiding over medhā
The anonymous commentator: «नोऽस्मान्प्रत्या[गादा]गच्छतु» — may she come to us
Sāyaṇa: «विश्वमञ्चतीति विश्वाची सर्वावगाहनक्षमेत्यर्थः» — able to enter into everything
The anonymous commentator: «शोभनं मनोऽस्मदनुग्राहकमिच्छन्ती» — wishing a kind mind towards us
The anonymous commentator: «पुरुषार्थानुपयोगिनो वेदबाह्या[ञ्शब्दा]न्» — words of no use to the aims of life, outside the Veda
The anonymous commentator: «बृहद्वदेम परब्रह्मतत्त्वं कथयामः» — may we speak of the supreme brahman

words.meaning: in the assembly, at the rite
words.context: The anonymous commentator: «विदथे यज्ञेऽनुष्ठिते सति शुद्धान्तःकरणा भूत्वा» — the sacrifice performed, our minds made pure
The anonymous commentator: «शोभनपुत्रशिष्यादिरूपा» — with good sons and pupils
The anonymous commentator: «ऋषिरतीन्द्रियदर्शी भवति» — one who sees beyond the senses
The anonymous commentator: «पुरुषो ब्रह्मा हिरण्यगर्भो भवति» — becomes Brahmā, Hiraṇyagarbha

words.meaning: one to whom fortune has come
words.context: The anonymous commentator: «आगतश्रीः प्राप्तसंपद्भवति» — one who has gained wealth
The anonymous commentator: «चित्रं गवाश्वहिरण्यधान्यादिकं विविधं» — of many kinds: cattle, horses, gold, grain

words.gram: m. nom. sg. (as read by the commentator)
words.context: The anonymous commentator: «द्रविणो न द्रविणपतिरिव। द्रविणशब्देन तत्पतिर्लक्ष्यते» — draviṇaḥ stands for the lord of wealth

sandhi.type: aḥ before a vowel; t before a voiced sound
sandhi.rule: naḥ + āgāt → na āgāt (P. 8.3.19 (लोपः शाकल्यस्य)); āgāt + viśvācī → āgād viśvācī (P. 8.2.39 (झलां जशोऽन्ते)).

sandhi.type: n before b; t before a voiced sound
sandhi.rule: n stays before b; bṛhat + vadema → bṛhad vadema.

sandhi.type: aḥ before a vowel; i-visarga before a voiced sound
sandhi.rule: juṣṭaḥ + ṛṣiḥ → juṣṭa ṛṣiḥ; ṛṣiḥ + bhavati → ṛṣir bhavati.

sandhi.type: ā + ā; ī-visarga before a vowel
sandhi.rule: brahmā + āgataśrīḥ → brahmāgataśrīḥ (P. 6.1.101 (अकः सवर्णे दीर्घः)), printed with a space after brahmā; āgataśrīḥ + uta → °śrīr uta.
The visarga becomes ś before c (P. 8.3.34 (विसर्जनीयस्य सः), P. 8.4.40 (स्तोः श्चुना श्चुः)).

samasa.meaning: one to whom fortune has come

morphology.note: The base prints brahmā gataśrīr, with a space; the letters are the same as brahmā āgataśrīḥ joined. The anonymous commentator and Sāyaṇa read āgataśrīḥ, ‘to whom fortune has come’; the Ānandāśrama text prints ब्रह्माऽऽगतश्रीः with the avagraha that marks the merged ā.
A root aorist of √gā with ā; the commentators read it as a wish (‘may she come’).

The anonymous commentator reads draviṇo na as ‘like the lord of wealth’; Sāyaṇa glosses ‘with wealth’ («द्रविणेन धनेन जुषस्व»), as if draviṇena, which is the reading of the Tirupati e-text (see flags).

translation.literal: Medhā, the goddess, favouring, has come to us — all-pervading, auspicious, well-disposed. Favoured by you, driving away ill-spoken words, may we speak the great in the assembly, with good sons. Favoured by you one becomes a seer, goddess; by you a Brahmā; one to whom fortune has come, also by you. Favoured by you one gains varied wealth. Such as you are, favour us, Medhā, like the lord of wealth.
translation.readable: May Medhā, the goddess, come to us gladly — she who reaches everywhere, auspicious and kind. Favoured by you, may we put away idle talk and speak of the highest at the rite, with good sons and pupils around us. By your favour, goddess, one becomes a seer; by your favour, a Brahmā; by your favour, prosperous; by your favour one finds wealth of every kind. Favour us, Medhā, as a lord of riches favours the poor.

anvaya: मेधा देवी विश्वाची भद्रा सुमनस्यमाना जुषमाणा नः आगात् । [देवि,] त्वया जुष्टाः दुरुक्तान् नुदमानाः सुवीराः [वयम्] विदथे बृहत् वदेम । देवि, त्वया जुष्टः ऋषिः भवति, त्वया ब्रह्मा, उत त्वया आगतश्रीः [भवति] । त्वया जुष्टः चित्रम् वसु विन्दते । मेधे, सा [त्वम्] द्रविणः न नः जुषस्व ।
syntax: Two verses. The first: a third-person statement or wish (āgāt) with the goddess as subject and four qualifying nominatives; then a first-person plural optative (vadema) with participles describing the speakers. The second: four short clauses with tvayā juṣṭaḥ (‘favoured by you’) and a predicate, the verb (bhavati) said once and understood; then an imperative (juṣasva) with a vocative and a comparison (draviṇo na).

ambiguities.note: ‘A Brahmā, to whom fortune has come’ (āgataśrīḥ, the commentators) or ‘a Brahmā who has gone to fortune’ (gataśrīḥ, as printed with a space).
‘Like the lord of wealth’ (the anonymous commentator) or ‘with wealth’ (Sāyaṇa’s gloss, matching the reading draviṇena).

The anonymous commentator and Sāyaṇa: the power to retain a text and its meaning, needed for the unbroken practice of the knowledge that the self is one with the Lord («जीवात्मन ईश्वरेणाभेदज्ञानं यदस्ति तस्य ज्ञानस्य नैरन्तर्येण साधनं मेधाधीनम्»).

metre.name: triṣṭubh
metre.note: Two triṣṭubh verses, each printed in two lines.

beginner: This is the opening of the hymn to Medhā — the goddess of understanding, and especially of the power to take in a teaching and keep it. The first verse asks her to come gladly, she who reaches everywhere, and says that with her favour we will stop speaking idle words and speak instead of the highest truth at the rite. The second verse lists what her favour brings: one becomes a seer who sees beyond the senses, one becomes a Brahmā, one becomes prosperous and finds wealth of every kind. It ends by asking her to favour us as a rich patron favours someone in need. The old commentators explain why the hymn stands here: the knowledge the Upaniṣad teaches has to be held in the mind without a break, and that depends on medhā.
analogy: Like asking for a good memory before learning a long poem by heart.

commentary.label: direct
commentary.text: It asks Medhā to come, and says that by her favour the speakers will drive away ill-spoken words and speak of the great at the rite; that by her favour one becomes a seer, a Brahmā, prosperous, and gains wealth; and it asks her to favour the speakers.

commentary.q: Why is medhā prayed for here?
commentary.label: traditional
commentary.text: The anonymous commentator: the three trisuparṇa removed the sins that obstruct knowledge; now, since keeping up the knowledge that the self is one with the Lord depends on medhā, the deity of medhā is invoked: «इत्थं प्रतिबन्धनिवृत्त्युपायमुक्त्वा जीवात्मन ईश्वरेणाभेदज्ञानं यदस्ति तस्य ज्ञानस्य नैरन्तर्येण साधनं मेधाधीनमतो मेधाभिमानिनीं देवतां प्रार्थयितुमेकामृचमाह». Sāyaṇa gives the same reason in nearly the same words.

commentary.label: traditional
commentary.text: Both the anonymous commentator and Sāyaṇa: the power to retain a text and its meaning, «ग्रन्थतदर्थयोर्धारणशक्तिर्मेधा».

commentary.q: How do the commentators rank the sins of the trisuparṇa?
commentary.label: traditional
commentary.text: Introducing this hymn, the anonymous commentator ranks the three sins the trisuparṇa remove: the killing of a brāhmaṇa is the gravest of the five great sins, the killing of an embryo graver, and the killing of a hero graver still; repeating the trisuparṇa for life removes even these: «ईदृशानामपि निवर्तको यावज्जीवं त्रिसुपर्णजपः». These are his claims about the text, reported as such.

commentary.label: traditional
commentary.text: The anonymous commentator: words of no use to the aims of life, outside the Veda, which the favoured speakers drive away, so that, the sacrifice done and their minds purified, they speak of the supreme brahman.

schools.disagreement: No Vedānta-school commentary on this text is in the edition’s sources. The anonymous commentator and Sāyaṇa connect medhā with the knowledge that the self is one with the Lord, an Advaita reading they give in passing; Bhāskara’s comments on this hymn (his anuvākas 39–42) are missing from the edition’s copy, and Raṅgarāmānuja’s commentary on the Mahānārāyaṇa is not among the sources.

contemporary.text: The hymn treats the ability to keep what one has learned as a gift to be asked for, not only a skill. Whatever one makes of the prayer, it marks how much depends on retaining a teaching, and not only on hearing it. This is a modern reflection on the passage, not part of its traditional meaning.

reflect.beginner: What is something you learned once and are glad you remembered?
reflect.deeper: The hymn asks to ‘drive away ill-spoken words’ in order to speak of the highest. What talk would you have to drop to speak of what matters most to you?
reflect.practice: After reading something worth keeping, close the page and say back to yourself what it said.

references.text: Sāyaṇa comments on this hymn as his anuvāka 39; the edition’s concordance maps it correctly. Bhāskara’s anuvākas 39–42, which would hold his comment, are not in the edition’s copy of his work.

flags.note: At the end of the hymn the Tirupati e-text reads draviṇena and omits medhe (corrections.json); the base and the Ānandāśrama text read draviṇo na medhe. Sāyaṇa’s gloss «द्रविणेन धनेन जुषस्व» matches the Tirupati reading; the base is kept.
brahmā gataśrīr is read as brahmā āgataśrīḥ with the commentators.
